# Whitsuntide

The thistles have colonized the mountainside again this year, their purple crowns nodding above the coarse grass like a congregation that has wandered off from some stricter, more orderly service. It is Whitsuntide, 2010, and the field itself seems to know something—some secret about descent, about tongues of fire landing not on the apostles but on these stubborn, thorned stalks that nobody planted and nobody will harvest. This is what accessibility looks like: a state of subtle shock, of quiet spiritual disruption, available to anyone who simply walks up the hill and stands still long enough to let it register. And yet how rarely anyone does. How rarely I do.

Because right now I am not on the mountainside. I am at my desk, and the temptation to leave—to abandon the glowing rectangle of the screen for the actual glowing rectangle of the sea, visible if I would only stand and walk to the window, or further, down the road—this temptation sits in me like a held breath. I could go. I could see the water do whatever water does on a morning like this. Instead I refresh the page. I watch the numbers. Microsystems, ticking, always ticking, and I am checking it with the compulsive rhythm of an addict counting hours until the next fix, except the fix is just information, just red or green, just the small electric jolt of knowing whether the number has moved and which direction.

Outside—I can see this much from where I sit—two redtail hawks are riding a thermal, spiraling upward without a single visible effort, wings set, patient, riding the invisible column of warm air as though the sky owed them this ascent. It should mean something uncomplicated. It should simply be beautiful. But even as I watch them lift and turn, some other part of my mind is superimposing the stock ticker onto their flight path, imagining the numbers themselves lifting like this, red draining into green, loss becoming gain on the same rising current, as if the market had its own thermals, its own patient predatory birds circling above the wreckage of somebody's portfolio.

Why does every moment feel like this—so overloaded, so doubled? Why does each instant carry simultaneously the charge of catastrophe and the charge of utopia, apocalypse braided with radical possibility, as though I cannot experience a single unadorned minute without also experiencing its opposite? I feel, in the same breath, that everything is about to collapse and that everything is about to open into some unprecedented freedom. I oscillate. I do not choose between these poles; they choose me, alternating with a speed that leaves me no time to settle into either one before the other arrives.

And I recognize, uncomfortably, that this is simply what my equilibrium is made of. There is no steady ground beneath the oscillation—there is only the oscillation itself, the collision and cancellation of extremities, mood crashing into countermood until something that resembles calm emerges, briefly, from the wreckage of their mutual negation. It is not peace. It is the temporary silence after two loud things have struck each other and gone quiet. I call this silence my balance, but I know better.

And the thistles keep spreading. In my mind now the field opens outward, past the mountainside, past the country, becoming the whole tilted surface of the earth—and what scatters across it is no longer purple flowerheads but currency, all of it, everywhere: dollars lifting in the wind like seedheads, solidi and yen and rand and rupees drifting down across furrows and rooftops and unmarked borders, a global thistle-field of money, ungathered, self-seeding, taking root in soil that never asked for it. My private oscillation, my small violent balance between the sea I am not walking to and the numbers I cannot stop checking, turns out to be only a local instance of something enormous—the whole world caught in its own red-to-green conversion, its own thermal of hope and collapse, spiraling upward on currents no one can see, going nowhere, unable to land.

# Whitsuntide, 2010

The mountain does nothing to hurry you. That was the first thing I noticed, sitting there on the worn granite outcrop above the tree line, the wind moving through early summer grass with a patience that seemed almost cruel in its indifference to human urgency. Whitsuntide had brought me here, ostensibly for rest, though rest was proving to be the most elusive thing I'd sought in years.

Below, the valley spread out in that particular green that only comes in late May—vivid, saturated, unbothered by anything except the slow work of photosynthesis and growth. A hawk turned in lazy circles somewhere to my left. The quiet had a texture to it, a thickness that pressed gently against the ears, and I found myself wanting to dissolve into it, to become simply another still thing among the rocks and scattered alpine flowers.

This was the pull I had come for: the transcendent quiet, the sense that here, at least, time moved according to a different logic than the one that governed my waking hours in the city. Nature does not check its phone. Nature does not refresh a page sixteen times in an hour, hunting for the small red or green numbers that might tell it whether the day was good or bad, whether the accumulated decisions of a lifetime were paying off or unraveling. Nature simply is, in a continuous unbroken present tense, and I had hoped that some of this steadiness might seep into me by proximity, the way heat passes from stone to skin.

And yet.

I felt it there, even on the mountainside—the phone a small dense weight in my jacket pocket, pulling at my attention with a gravity that had nothing to do with its actual mass. The markets were open, technically, somewhere in another time zone, and some restless part of my mind kept circling back to numbers I had looked at that morning, wondering if they had moved, wondering what news might have broken, wondering whether the small emotional architecture I had built around a modest portfolio might have shifted while I sat here pretending to seek peace.

This was the other pull, the shadow pull: not steady but spiking, not continuous but staccato, a rhythm of anxiety and relief and anxiety again that had nothing of the mountain's patience in it. Checking the markets did not offer presence—it offered only the illusion of control, a brief hit of information that satisfied nothing but generated instead a new itch, a new uncertainty to be resolved by checking again. It was addiction in miniature, the compulsive return to a source that never truly satisfies, that only trains the nervous system to crave the next glance, the next update, the next small verdict rendered in percentage points.

I sat with this contradiction for a long while, watching the hawk, feeling the phone's weight, aware of how strange it was that both pulls could coexist within the same quiet hour on the same quiet mountain. The world had constructed for me two entirely different modes of attention: one that asked for nothing and gave everything, and another that promised everything and gave, in truth, almost nothing—just the recursive loop of checking, a hollow ritual dressed up as vigilance, as responsibility, as prudence.

What troubled me most was not the existence of this tension but its persistence, its refusal to resolve itself simply because I had removed myself physically to a place of supposed sanctuary. The mountain's silence did not cancel out the market's noise; instead, the two coexisted, layered atop one another, each vying for the same finite attention I possessed. I understood, sitting there, that this was perhaps the defining psychological condition of the era—not that we lacked access to peace, but that we had built compulsive machinery capable of intruding upon peace even in its most literal, physical presence. Even here, three thousand feet up, with wind and grass and the ancient patience of rock all around me, some small addictive circuit in my mind kept reaching for a screen.

I did not check the phone, in the end—not for those particular hours, at least. But I noted the reaching, the way the impulse rose and fell like a wave, disturbing what might otherwise have been an unbroken surface. And I understood that this was the real work of contemplation now, in this particular decade: not simply to seek stillness, but to notice, without judgment, how readily and how often stillness was interrupted by the small anxious machinery we had built and now carried with us everywhere, even to the tops of mountains, even into moments meant for something entirely other than counting.

# May and Whitsuntide

May has long held a special place in the calendar of the changing seasons, marking that vibrant transition when spring reaches its fullest expression and the promise of summer draws near. Trees don full canopies of green, hedgerows fill with hawthorn blossom, and the countryside awakens with birdsong and new growth. It is a month steeped in folklore and celebration, from May Day festivities with their maypoles and garlands to the quieter joys of long, light-filled evenings.

Within this season falls Whitsuntide, one of the great festivals of the Christian year. Taking its name from "White Sunday"—so called for the white garments traditionally worn by those newly baptized at this time—Whitsuntide commemorates Pentecost, the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles fifty days after Easter. Because Easter itself moves according to the lunar calendar, Whitsuntide falls at different points each year, though it most often lands within May, sometimes stretching into early June.

Historically, Whitsuntide was celebrated with considerable festivity across Britain and much of Europe. Whit walks, fairs, and church processions filled towns and villages, while Whit Monday became an important holiday for workers, offering a welcome pause in the agricultural and industrial calendar. Morris dancing, well-dressing, and other folk customs often found their expression during this period, blending pre-Christian seasonal celebration with Christian observance in ways typical of English tradition.

The connection between May and Whitsuntide reflects a broader pattern found throughout the ritual year: the layering of natural, agricultural rhythms with religious meaning. Just as May itself represents renewal and fertility in the natural world, Whitsuntide's message of spiritual renewal—the Spirit's arrival bringing new courage and purpose to the apostles—resonates with the same themes of rebirth and possibility.

Though many of the old Whitsuntide customs have faded in modern times, replaced by different holiday patterns and shifting religious observance, the season retains its quiet significance. May remains a month of transformation, and Whitsuntide, whenever it falls within it, continues to carry echoes of centuries of celebration, faith, and the deep human impulse to mark the turning of the year with meaning and joy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem mixing nature imagery with stock market anxiety, set on a specific date in 2010.
counterfactuals.output:
# May 6, 2010

The crocuses knew before I did, closing their throats at 2:32 in the afternoon like something ancient sensing weather that hadn't arrived yet, and I was watching the ticker the way you watch a hawk circle—not knowing if it's hunting or just riding thermals, just being a hawk, just doing hawk things while your portfolio does whatever the digital equivalent of falling out of the sky looks like, nine hundred points, a thousand, gone into some algorithmic wind shear nobody could name yet they'd call it the Flash Crash later like a superhero's origin story except the hero never showed and the villain was just math, just fear moving at the speed of light through fiber optic cable buried under the same earth where earthworms don't know a single thing about Procter & Gamble trading at a penny, at zero, at prices that shouldn't exist in any universe with physical laws—

and outside my window the maple doesn't care, drops its helicopter seeds in lazy spirals, samaras they're called, I looked it up once, small persistent parachutes of continuation, of next year, while inside the machines I don't understand were unwinding decades in minutes, and somewhere a pension fund manager is watching his hands shake like aspen leaves in wind that isn't there yet, that's coming, that's always coming—

the way a doe freezes not from the sound but from the silence after, the too-quiet quiet, the market doing its version of that stillness, that terrible held breath before the exchanges just stopped, just closed their eyes for eighteen minutes like a held breath, like a heron standing one-legged in water pretending to be reeds, pretending stillness is the same as safety, and maybe it is, maybe cash is just standing very still in tall grass hoping the predator passes—

by 3:00 it was clawing back, the number climbing like ivy finds sunlight, blind and persistent, doesn't know it's climbing, just grows toward light because that's what it does, the way money tries to find yield the way water finds the crack in foundation, the path of least resistance downward always downward except when it's not, except when some invisible hand (not the one Adam Smith meant, some other hand, colder, coded) yanks it back up like a hawk pulling out of a dive at the last possible second, wings catching air, catching light, catching whatever the last algorithm decided real value was in that half-second—

and I thought: this is just weather. This is just the market being a season unto itself, spring coming in fits, false starts, that one warm week in February when everything blooms too early and then the frost comes back to kill the blossoms, the plum trees fooled every single year and every single year they try again anyway, that stubborn hope written into cellular memory, into rings we won't see until the tree is cut open decades from now, someone counting backward to this exact Thursday, this exact tremor, this day the numbers forgot what they meant and then remembered, mostly, close enough, close enough to call it recovery—

the crocuses opened again the next morning like nothing happened. Like they hadn't just performed the exact same panic in miniature, in purple, in silence, before the humans even knew to be afraid.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, Ashbery-style poem about thistles, hawks, Whitsuntide, and the manic energy of day-trading, with fragmented syntax and glitchy formatting.
counterfactuals.output:
# Thistle Ledger, Whit Monday

The hawk keeps its position above the index
of weeds—thistle, thistle, a purple static
in the field's margins, un-
sponsored content drifting where the harrow
didn't reach. Someone said *rotate sectors*
and the crows agreed, lifting
off the fence line like a sell signal
nobody wanted to read correctly.

Whitsuntide arrives without
                    quotation marks
the way Tuesday arrives, the way
a candle in the old rite meant *descent*
and now it means the market opening
in Tokyo while we sleep, tongues
of fire on every terminal, small
and green, small and red, the Spirit
moving on the face of the ticker

—thistle down and data down,
both refusing to be gathered
into anything you could call
a harvest. The hawk doesn't care
about your portfolio. It cares
about the vole's tremor in tall
grass, a signal purer than
whatever you're
                                        watching
                                        watching
                                        refresh—

Pentecost was supposed to mean
understanding across all tongues at once,
but today it means the fear
in every language sounds
the same on the desk: *sell sell
hold no sell*. The bells
in the village do their scheduled
thing, bronze and slow, uncorrelated
to anything, a rally
of sound that costs nothing
and returns nothing, which is
its whole late-medieval point—

Thistle: nature's own
short position, betting against
the smooth field, against
the mono-crop of intention.
It wins by lingering. It wins
by being the thing the scythe
resents and the finch
adores, that soft seed-parachute
economy, that IPO
of down feathers going
public in the wind for free—

And the hawk—the hawk is not
a metaphor for capital,
I keep telling myself, though it hovers
with such punctuational precision,
a colon in the sky before the swoop's
long sentence—

Whit Sunday, Whit Monday, the whole
liturgical week bleeding into
the trading week, candles into
candlesticks, red and green
on every chart, on every
chasuble, the priest's stole
doing what the moving average
does—marking a color
onto time, saying *here,
here is where the spirit / the price
moved through and touched us
and was gone before we
could name it rightly—*

Late in the day the field goes
gold-grey, thistles
shutting their small violet
fists, the hawk gone home
to wherever hawks
reconcile their accounts,
and somewhere a bell
for Compline, somewhere
a market closing in red
ink that will not wash out
by morning, by Monday,
by Pentecost's slow
insistence that the fire
was always meant to be
divided, tongue
by tongue by tongue by tongue—
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal internal monologue for someone torn between nature's stillness and the addictive pull of watching microsystems stocks, incorporating theological and apocalyptic language.
counterfactuals.output:
The pond does not refresh. This is its miracle. I sit before it and nothing loads, nothing ticks, and for a moment I understand what the mystics meant by *stillness*—the water holding its single green thought, unhurried, unbought.

Then the phone in my pocket becomes a small sun and I feel it before I hear it, the way the faithful must have felt the first trumpet.

MSFT down four cents.

I do not want to look. I am Lot's wife with her neck already turning, already becoming the pillar of something white and mineral and useless. Behind me the garden. Ahead of me the numbers, the numbers, the numbers—a burning bush that does not speak but *blinks*, green then red then green, an oracle in decimal points, and I am Moses asking it for a name and it gives me only *volume* and *volatility* and I take off my shoes anyway because some ground is holy even when it lies.

The candlesticks on the chart look like a city on fire seen from very far away. I think: this is what Sodom looked like to the two angels walking uphill, not turning back, obedient, boring, saved. I am not obedient. I keep the tab open in another window like a second heart, arrhythmic, tithing my attention to it every four minutes, my rosary counted in refreshes.

The trees do not report quarterly earnings. This should comfort me. Instead I feel the old itch, the manna-hoarding sin—give us this day our daily bread and also let us keep some for tomorrow, let us stockpile the miracle, let us index it, diversify the loaves and fishes across several small-cap baskets just in case God's dividend disappoints.

A crow lands on the fence and regards me with one black unblinking eye, the eye of an auditor, the eye of a recording angel keeping ledgers no accountant will ever see. *You could just watch the water,* the crow does not say, because crows do not speak, but I hear it anyway the way you hear your own conscience wearing a stranger's voice.

Somewhere a small tech company I have never used loses eleven percent of itself in an afternoon and I feel this in my ribs like a rapture that only some of us were called to, an elect group of shareholders lifted briefly into green numbers before the inevitable correction drags us back down into flesh, into portfolios, into the long tribulation of Mondays.

I want the pond's patience. I want to be the kind of creature who does not need an apocalypse every four minutes to feel alive, who can sit in unbought stillness and call it enough, call it *very good*, the way God did on the seventh day before he too, presumably, checked his phone.

But the ticker is a testament and I am still reading it, still hungry for its small continuous endings, its daily little Armageddons that never quite arrive, that promise arrival, that keep me here on this bench between the water and the fire, unable to choose the garden, unable to leave it either, my thumb hovering like a dove that has seen the olive branch and decided, after all, to stay in the air a little longer—just to see what happens next.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental fiction/poetry hybrid that uses currency symbols (yen, rand, rupees) and natural imagery (thistles, hawks, wind) to explore emotional instability and the search for "balance."
counterfactuals.output:
# LEDGER FOR AN UNSTEADY HEART

*rate fixed to nothing, floating against everything*

---

**I. Opening Balance**

¥en — the old word for wanting,
before it was money, was only *ache,*
a coin minted from craving and called currency
so the ache could be counted, exchanged, spent.

I have been spending myself all week.

Some days I am worth ₹100 to the ₹1,
generous, inflated, giving the whole sky away —
some days I am ₽ collapsed against every hawk-shadow,
worth less than the wind it takes to say my name.

---

**II. The Thistle Accounts**

    debit: softness
    credit: barb

The thistle does not apologize
for the way it refuses the hand.
Purple-headed, ledger-straight,
it stands in the field converting
sun into spite, spite into stem,
and calls this *growing.*

I understand the thistle.
I have also turned tenderness
into something that draws blood
just to prove it was real.

No currency for that.
No exchange rate between
*I loved you* and *I could not stop bristling.*

---

**III. Hawk, Held**

The hawk hangs in moving air —
not still, but *stilled,*
a decision made forty times a second
against a wind that has no decisions at all.

This is the only balance I have witnessed:
not the absence of falling
but the practiced argument against it,
wingtip by wingtip,
¥ against ₹ against ₽,
each correction smaller than the last mistake.

Below, the field of thistles doesn't move.
Above, everything is negotiation.

---

**IV. Exchange Rate, Live**

     ¥ 147.32 ⇌ ₹ 1.00      (rising)
     ₹ 1.00   ⇌ ₽ 0.98      (falling)
     ₽ 0.98   ⇌ ¥ 147.32   (correcting, always correcting)

this is not about money
this is about the hour I wake up
generous as ¥en, wide as a country's worth of want
and the hour, same day, I am
₽ devalued, worthless even to the hawk
who does not eat what cannot fight the wind

somewhere between these hours
is a number
I have never once landed on

---

**V. Wind, Unaccountable**

Wind has no denomination.
It cannot be converted, hoarded, spent.
It simply *is,* moving through the thistle-field,
lifting the hawk, bending nothing that will not bend,
snapping nothing that insists on rigidity.

Maybe that's the lesson the field keeps giving me
and I keep failing to bank:

not the thistle's stubbornness,
not the coin's anxious math,
not even the hawk's small, endless corrections —

but the wind's indifference to being owed anything at all.

---

**VI. Closing Balance**

I want to tell you I found it —
the rate that holds,
¥ = ₹ = ₽ = *steady*,
some gold standard for the self.

I didn't.

But some evenings the hawk still hangs there,
correcting, correcting,
worth exactly what the moment asks of it —
no more, no less —

and I think: *maybe that's not balance.
Maybe that's just staying aloft
long enough to call it living.*

The thistles don't care either way.
The wind cashes nothing.
I am still counting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
